To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

family ownership creates more value than nonfamily ownership when the founder serves in the CEO position, that family control destroys value when the founder is the CEO, and that family management destroys value when the CEO is the founder's descendant.
family ownership is associated with higher firm value than nonfamily ownership, family control reduces the value of family ownership, and family management reduces firm value.
the value of family firms depends on whether they are founder controlled and managed or descendant controlled and managed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the three fundamental elements of family firms affect the value of the firm and the costs of the owner manager conflict.
how ownership management and control affect firm value and how the value of family ownership varies depending on who is the CEO of the firm.
the fundamental question: how do family ownership management and control affect firm value?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
family ownership is not necessarily a value enhancing factor for firms, but family management and control are.
, on average, family ownership creates value when the founder serves in a control position and destroys value when the founder or his descendants manage the firm.
family ownership and control create value only in founder controlled firms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the founder CEO family firms are more valuable than the nonfamily firms, while the descendant CEO family firms are less valuable than non-family firms.
, in order for family ownership to create value, the founder must be the firm's CEO or the Chairman.
the founder CEO is the only family firm structure that creates value, and even then the founder's premium is not very large, and that the value destruction from descendant CEO firms is very large.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, to understand the value of family firms and their differences from nonfamily firms, we must distinguish among three dimensions of the family firm definition: ownership, control and management.
the value implications of family ownership are not straightforward.

, in order for the family firm literature to make meaningful progress, researchers should be more explicit about the elements of family firms that are being studied and should use more sophisticated proxies to identify these elements.
